Maladaptive Strategies.value: Any form of physical contact with others
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

vignette:
Mark presents as a 36-year-old tax consultant, married for seven years, who moves with a rigid tension that seems at odds with his quiet, professional demeanor. His military service ended eight years ago, but the events of his final tour in Afghanistan have become more, not less, present in his daily life. The index trauma occurred during a foot patrol outside a small village. After a tense meeting with local elders-a conversation that went nowhere-his unit was moving through an eerily quiet alleyway. Mark remembers the oppressive heat making him feel nauseous and dizzy, the gritty taste of dust coating his tongue, and the sudden, profound silence just before the IED detonated. He was thrown against a wall, biting his tongue so hard he tasted blood mixed with the dust.

In the years since, these sensory details have become potent hooks. At his firm, a client raising their voice in a confrontational manner over an audit notice is no longer just a difficult conversation; it's a trigger that instantly brings back a fragmented memory of the argument with the village elders (Triggers -> Memory). With the memory comes the metallic taste of blood and dust, so vivid it makes him gag (Memory -> Taste Vividness). The emotional wave that follows is overwhelming, a suffocating panic that feels identical to the moment of the blast. To manage this, Mark has developed a rigid set of strategies. He will abruptly end the confrontational meeting, citing a sudden need to retrieve a file, and then avoid speaking to that client for days, communicating only through terse emails (Triggers -> Maladaptive Strategies). He has come to believe that talking about what happened, or even showing strong emotion, will cause him to lose control completely.

This pattern of avoidance has become the central organizing principle of his life. At home, his wife Sarah has learned not to ask about his time in the service, as any such conversation topic causes him to shut down entirely (Triggers -> Maladaptive Strategies). The memories themselves are so powerful that they fuel his deep-seated conviction that he is in constant danger (Memory -> Threat). When an image of the alleyway flashes into his mind, he immediately begins scanning whatever room he is in, plotting his escape routes through windows or secondary doors. This constant hypervigilance, in turn, makes the memories more accessible; the state of high alert primes him to see threats everywhere, and any perceived threat can bring the memories rushing back (Threat -> Memory). A moment of unusual silence in his normally bustling office can feel so menacing that it conjures the image of that quiet alleyway just before the explosion (Threat -> Triggers).

The strategies Mark employs to keep the memories at bay have paradoxically strengthened their hold and amplified his sense of threat. By refusing to talk about the trauma, he ensures the memories remain fragmented, unprocessed, and emotionally raw, making them more likely to intrude with overwhelming force (Maladaptive Strategies -> Memory). His avoidance of any physical touch is particularly damaging to his marriage. When Sarah reaches for him unexpectedly, he flinches violently, a physiological alarm response he cannot control (Threat -> Startle to Touch). He then retreats, leaving her feeling rejected and confused (Memory -> Maladaptive Strategies). This self-imposed isolation has made him exquisitely sensitive to his environment; the lack of physical comfort and connection makes the world feel sharper and more dangerous, increasing his general state of threat (Maladaptive Strategies -> Threat).

Lately, the cycle has become almost constant. Even feeling physically unwell with a common cold can now trigger the memory of the heat-induced nausea he felt that day (Triggers -> Memory). This memory then reinforces his fear that his body is failing him and that he is unsafe (Memory -> Threat), which makes him even more sensitive to any future triggers, like a tense phone call at work (Memory -> Triggers). He has also started to actively push away any positive feelings, viewing them as a dangerous lapse in vigilance. A moment of genuine laughter with a colleague feels so unsafe that he immediately finds a reason to retreat to his office, where he can feel the familiar, protective numbness return. This constant effort to suppress and avoid has made him more likely to misinterpret neutral events as threatening, which then serves as a trigger for the entire cycle to begin again (Maladaptive Strategies -> Triggers). Sometimes, the memory comes back without any feeling at all; he can see the events unfold with a cold, detached clarity, as if watching a film about a stranger, a state that frightens him more than the panic.

Mark sought therapy after his wife told him, her voice quiet with grief, that she felt she was "living with a ghost." The statement broke through his emotional armor, forcing him to confront the reality that his strategies for survival were destroying the life he had survived for. He is terrified of losing his wife and his career, but he is more terrified of the memories themselves, believing that if he ever truly lets them in, they will annihilate him completely.
